reason: Two independent, authoritative sources corroborate essentially every material claim in the description. (1) Taiwan Business TOPICS (AMCham Taiwan), "Taiwan Reaps Harvest of Rural Finance Reform," confirms nearly verbatim: in the first half of 1995 capital-market volatility triggered a liquidity shortage causing "panic runs on some of the weakest credit departments"; Taiwan had ~300 farmers'/fishermen's associations operating ~1,160 credit departments; NPL rates rose from 8.6% (1996) to 15.5% (2004); deposit market share fell from 11% to 7% over the same period; the 2003 Agricultural Finance Act put credit departments under the Council of Agriculture's Bureau of Agricultural Finance; and the 2005 creation of the Agricultural Bank of Taiwan (BOAF-established, 49% government-owned) followed. (2) An official 1998 speech by the Chairman of Taiwan's Central Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC), a primary regulatory source, independently states: "During the first half of 1995, huge fluctuations in Taiwan's financial markets gave rise to insufficient liquidity. This led to a small number of the weaker credit departments of farmers' associations experiencing panic runs. Depositors thus lost confidence in these associations, and their financial market share consequently declined" — and details that beginning July 1995, 14 credit departments experienced runs, with CDIC/competent authorities dispatching supervisory task forces to take charge of problem institutions' day-to-day operations (matching the "placed under state administration" claim), plus deposit market share data (11.1% in 1995 to 10.5% in 1996) consistent with the described longer-run decline to 7%. Every checkable specific (year, mechanism, association/unit counts, NPL trajectory, deposit-share trajectory, 2003 Act, 2005 Agricultural Bank of Taiwan) is corroborated by these independent sources with no contradicting evidence found.
